summary: Jesus sends seventy disciples ahead of Him two by two. They return rejoicing that demons obeyed them; He points them to a greater joy: names written in heaven.
key_insight: The Seventy came back excited that demons obeyed them. Jesus told them to rejoice instead that their names were written in heaven. Then He Himself “rejoiced in the Spirit,” not over power, but over the Father revealing Himself to babes.
story: The Lord appointed seventy others and sent them out two by two ahead of Him, into every town and place where He was about to go. “The harvest truly is great, but the laborers are few,” He told them; “therefore pray the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into His harvest. Go your way; behold, I send you out as lambs among wolves.”

They were to travel light, with no money bag, knapsack or sandals, and not stop to greet people along the road. In any house they entered, they were to say first, “Peace to this house,” and stay there, eating what they were given, “for the laborer is worthy of his wages.” In a town that welcomed them they were to heal the sick and say, “The kingdom of God has come near to you.” If a town refused them, they were to wipe its very dust off their feet as a warning. It would be more tolerable for Sodom in that Day than for that town.

Then Jesus spoke of the towns that had seen His mighty works and not repented: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!” If Tyre and Sidon had seen such works, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. And Capernaum, lifted up to heaven, would be brought down to Hades. “He who hears you hears Me,” He said, “he who rejects you rejects Me, and he who rejects Me rejects Him who sent Me.”

The seventy returned with joy: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in Your name.” Jesus said, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.” He had given them authority over all the power of the enemy. “Nevertheless do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rather rejoice because your names are written in heaven.”

In that hour Jesus rejoiced in the Spirit and said, “I thank You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to babes.” All things had been handed over to Him by His Father. No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him.

Then He turned to His disciples and said privately, “Blessed are the eyes which see the things you see.” Many prophets and kings had longed to see and hear what they were seeing and hearing, and had not.

scene.label: Seventy
scene.text: The number may recall the seventy elders who shared Moses’ work (Numbers 11:16–25), or the seventy nations listed in Genesis 10. Some manuscripts of Luke read seventy-two, which is also the count of nations in the Greek Old Testament; the NKJV follows those that read seventy.

scene.label: No greetings on the road
scene.text: Greetings in the East could be long and formal. When Elisha sent his servant on an urgent errand, he told him, “If you meet anyone, do not greet him” (2 Kings 4:29). The Seventy were on that kind of errand.

scene.label: A son of peace
scene.text: This is a Hebrew way of describing someone marked by a quality, here a person ready to receive God’s peace. “Peace” was an everyday greeting, but on these messengers’ lips it announced the kingdom.

scene.label: Chorazin, Bethsaida, Capernaum
scene.text: Three towns within a few miles of each other at the north end of the Sea of Galilee. The Gospels record no miracle in Chorazin, yet Jesus says many were done there. Tyre and Sidon were pagan ports the prophets had condemned (Ezekiel 26–28).

witnesses.luke: Only Luke records the sending of the Seventy. A wider circle than the Twelve is sent ahead of Jesus, a first glimpse of the mission Luke follows in Acts, and only Luke tells us that Jesus “rejoiced in the Spirit.” Matthew records the woes and the prayer of thanks in another setting (Matthew 11:20–27); Jesus may well have spoken such words more than once.

seeing.reveals: Jesus sends ordinary followers with His own authority, so that hearing them is hearing Him. He sees Satan’s fall in their small mission, and He rejoices that the Father reveals Himself to the humble.
seeing.living: Jesus’ first instruction to the people He sent was to pray for more workers. Ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers, and expect to be one of them. When God uses you, let your deepest joy be not what you did but that your name is written in heaven.
seeing.ponder: What makes you glad in serving God: what happens through you, or that you belong to Him?

preaching.big_idea: Rejoice less in what God does through you than in what He has done for you.
preaching.watch_for: The passage opens with prayer for laborers (v. 2) and closes with Jesus’ own prayer of thanks (v. 21). Between them, joy moves from the disciples’ success to the Father’s grace.
